draft.title: Purity in Shinto
card: In Shinto, purity means being clean and free from impurity. Impurity is not the same as sin. It is a kind of pollution, such as that linked to death, illness or wrongdoing, which can be removed.
Sincerity matters as well. Worshippers are expected to approach the kami with an honest and open heart.
Cleansing rituals remove impurity before people approach the kami. Examples are washing the hands and mouth with water at a shrine, and a purification rite led by a priest.
Purity matters because the kami are linked with what is clean and bright. Being cleansed lets a person come before them in a fitting state.
draft.remember: Impurity can be cleansed away, and worshippers come to the kami clean and sincere.

a.q: Why do worshippers wash their hands and mouth at a shrine?
opts: To remove impurity before approaching the kami
To pay the kami for answering a prayer
To confess sins so the kami will forgive them
To show that they belong to the shrine's priesthood
a.why: Washing is a cleansing ritual that removes impurity before worshippers come near the kami. It is not a confession of sins, because impurity in Shinto is pollution that can be cleansed, not sin.
a.clue: Think about what must happen before approaching the kami.

b.q: Haruto visits a shrine after a family funeral. He asks a priest to perform a purification rite. Which belief about impurity does this show?
opts: Impurity linked to death is pollution that can be removed
Impurity shows that a person has angered the kami
Impurity is a lasting fault that cannot be cleansed
Impurity only matters for priests and not for worshippers
b.why: Shinto treats impurity, including that linked with death, as pollution that a rite can remove. The tempting option says the kami are angered, but the card describes impurity as pollution, not as a sign of anger or sin.
b.clue: Impurity is a kind of pollution, not a sin.

a.best: To remove impurity before approaching the kami

b.best: Impurity linked to death is pollution that can be removed

Saying Haruto visits a shrine 'after a family funeral' may give a slightly misleading picture. Consider 'after the mourning period following a family funeral' or having the priest perform the rite elsewhere.
